method: behavioural: playback of broadband noise, position of shrimp in the tank scored

source.title: Annoying noise: effect of anthropogenic underwater noise on the movement and feeding performance in the red cherry shrimp, Neocaridina davidi

where: Abstract (sentence pair read on two fetches of the Frontiers article page; Methods for the stimulus)
quote: The spatial distribution of shrimp in response to the sound treatment showed significant changes; shrimp spent more time at the farthest one-third position from the sound source.
note: Pressure-only exposure in a small tank, so the response cannot be assigned to pressure or particle motion, and a behavioural change is not a hearing threshold. method: behavioural: grazing incubations on a motile alga with and without noise playback
conditions: Laboratory, 24 h incubations in the dark at 18 ± 0.2 °C; adults and copepodites from a lagoon at Büsum, Germany; 688 copepods (343 noise, 345 ambient); playback 174 dB re 1 µPa2 per Hz against ambient aquarium 155; most energy 100 to 2000 Hz; only the pressure component measured; prey Tetraselmis chuii; 51 vials (26 ambient, 25 noise), 7 to 19 copepods each, on a 1 rpm plankton wheel in a 130 L aquarium; one 20 min Büsum harbour recording (four boat passages) looped

source.authors: Kühn S, King F, Heubel K
source.title: Decreased feeding rates of the copepod Acartia tonsa when exposed to playback harbor traffic noise

where: Abstract (quoted sentence); Results text and Table 3 for density means, Table 4 for model selection
quote: We measured significantly decreased ingestion rates and clearance rates of A. tonsa when exposed to harbor noise compared to ambient conditions.
note: Feeding change shows the copepods are affected by sound, not what they hear or at what level; mechanism (masking of prey cues, distraction, physiology) is open. Handling time did not differ between sound treatments (p = 0.9). Mean ingestion was 48, 24, 64, 48 and 29% lower under noise at the five densities (Table 3). The authors kept the additive noise + prey density model for its fewer parameters, although the interaction model ranked first by AIC, and report no interaction test. Clearance was fitted with the Rogers random predator equation; noise lowered the capture rate (t = -3.7, p < 0.001). Taxonomy: Acartia (Acanthacartia) tonsa, accepted in WoRMS (AphiaID 104262, as shown on OBIS); Acartiidae, Calanoida, Copepoda. Crossref licence CC BY 4.0 (vor).

method: electroretinography with quasi-monochromatic LED stimulation; spectral sensitivity fitted with UV and green visual templates
conditions: Electroretinography on 16 eye preparations (12 female, 4 male); custom light source of 14 quasi-monochromatic LEDs, photon flux 2.4e11 to 2.4e15 photons per cm2 per s
quote: The spectral sensitivity of the compound eyes is bimodal with peaks at 370 nm (UV) and 526 nm (green).
note: Results give the fitted template peaks as 370.1 nm (UV) and 526.3 nm (green); female (12) and male (4) preparations did not differ significantly and were pooled. Taxonomy: Lycoriella ingenua (Dufour, 1839) accepted in the Catalogue of Life as shown on GBIF (gbif.org/species/1485806) and in GBIF species 143811283. value: attraction to light as a function of wavelength depends on light intensity
method: behavioural phototaxis in two designs: (1) single-wavelength stimuli at 11 wavelengths (368 to 637 nm), minimum photon flux needed for a response; (2) hexagonal choice box with UV 398, blue 447, green 512, red 631 nm and warm white at one constant intensity
conditions: Experiment 1: 1834 gnats in 50 trials (30 to 44 per trial), 30 s stimuli at 4 to 5 intensities, centroid bias scored; experiment 2: 50 dark-adapted gnats per trial, N = 1000 to 2000 per trial type, 2.7e13 photons per cm2 per s, 45 min; experiment 2 sample was 76% L. ingenua, 19% L. agraria, 5% other Lycoriella; sex not stated for behavioural trials; Catalogue of Life (via GBIF 1485806) lists L. agraria as a synonym of L. ingenua
quote: Behavioural experiments showed that attraction to light as a function of wavelength depends on light intensity.
note: At the threshold-intensity design the action spectrum peaked in the green (526.6 nm, template fit); at the higher constant intensity UV (398 nm) drew most gnats (60.98% of 622 choosers in type 1 trials), and green was most attractive where UV was absent (41.26%). No direct test of green against UV is reported for experiment 1, and the authors suggest ocelli may have affected experiment 1. Behavioural peak (about 526 nm) differs from the ERG UV peak. No p-value adjustment in experiment 1 (experiment 2 used Games-Howell and Tukey post hoc tests). Taxonomy as for the ERG records (Catalogue of Life via GBIF).
